newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai 1997 inflation seen higher but under control.
newsitem.headline: Thai 1997 inflation seen higher but under control.

text.p: The significant depreciation of the baht since its managed flotation will likely fuel Thai inflation this year, but it should remain at a manageable level, economists said on Friday.
They warned, however, that Thailand should brace for more pronounced inflationary pressure next year as the full effects of a cheaper baht set in.
Economists' projections for the inflation rate ranged from 5.5-7.0 percent for this year and 6.0-9.5 percent for 1998.

The official Thai government projection for inflation this year is 4.5 percent, compared to 5.8 percent in 1996, but this forecast was made before the government decided to free up the baht on July 2 in what amounted to a de facto devaluation.

Chances that Thailand's minimum wage may be adjusted by the end of next month, and signs of a drought in the making could make it harder for the government to keep inflation at bay, the economists said.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett, suggested the government should wait two to three months after the baht float to see a more solid trend for consumer prices.
"Based on our projection, one percent of devaluation in the currency works out to about 0.1-0.15 percent increase in the CPI," he said.

"I am quite optimistic. Although the economic picture remains foggy, we are still confident that demand will continue moderate. It's the prospect of drought that I'm worried about," he said. A dry spell has hit parts of Thailand.

Varut Siwasariyanon, head of research at ING Barings, said the government was likely to try to maintain price stability, otherwise interest rates would not come down and help revive the sluggish economy.
Thailand is going through its worst economic slump in more than a decade, with its ailing finance and property sectors hit hard by tight liquidity and poor asset qualities.
The Bank of Thailand on July 2 scrapped the tightly controlled basket-determined exchange regime and replaced it with a managed float system.
The baht has fallen to around 29.00-30.00 baht per dollar from around 25.10 baht before the float.
The central bank hoped that the baht flotation would encourage much-needed foreign inflows to alleviate the liquidity crunch and bring interest rates down.
The weaker baht has prompted concerns that consumer prices will rise on higher production costs due to rising imported content and increases in oil prices.
But Arporn Chewakengkrai of Deutsche Morgan Grenfrell said the higher inflation was likely to be cost-driven rather than demand-driven.
"My projection is the inflation for the whole of 1997 will not exceed 6.5 percent. Sluggish domestic demand will help ease pressure on prices," she said.
"Besides, during the first six months of 1997, inflation was only 4.4 percent, which is quite low," she said.

The government has indirectly intervened to control prices by asking oil companies to raise pump prices in stages in order to delay the effect of higher costs. It has also warned consumer goods dealers against profiteering.
It also spent some money from the government-controlled oil fund to subsidise prices of LPG, widely for cooking.
However, the government's ability to maintain fiscal and monetary disciplines will be a key to controlling inflation, said Chalongphob Sussangkarn of Thailand Development Research Institute (TDRI).

Although the TDRI forecast inflation for 1997 at around 6.8 percent, Chalongphob said the country could face hyperinflation of Latin American proportions if the government failed to effectively manage fiscal and monetary policy.
"Hyperinflation is possible if prices keep rising with the index to create an unending inflationary cycle...We have to be careful not to get ourselves into that cycle,' he said.
